analysis.subject: earth-science
analysis.pageCoverage: Page covers what a 100-year flood means, recurrence intervals and annual exceedance probability, how hydrologists use historical streamflow and rainfall data with frequency analysis, factors that determine if a storm produces a flood, and definitions of flood terms.

overview.headline: What a 100-year flood means and how flood probability is estimated

keyPoints.point: A flood with a 100-year recurrence interval has a 1 percent chance of occurring in any given year.
keyPoints.quote: In other words, a flood of that magnitude has a 1 percent chance of happening in any year.

keyPoints.point: Recurrence interval is based on the probability that an event will be equaled or exceeded in any year.
keyPoints.quote: The recurrence interval is based on the probability that the given event will be equaled or exceeded in any given year.

keyPoints.point: Frequency analysis estimates the probability of rainfall and streamflow and determines recurrence intervals.
keyPoints.quote: Ten or more years of data are required to perform a frequency analysis for the determination of recurrence intervals.

keyPoints.point: A 100-year storm does not always cause a 100-year flood because rainfall distribution, soil saturation and streamflow response differ.
keyPoints.quote: Several factors can independently influence the cause-and-effect relation between rainfall and streamflow.

keyPoints.point: The 100-year flood level can change as more data are collected or when dams and development alter river flow.
keyPoints.quote: Since the 100-year flood level is statistically computed using past, existing data, as more data comes in, the level of the 100-year flood will change

keyTerms.gloss: average years between floods of a given size used to describe flood probability
keyTerms.quote: The average number of years between floods of a certain size is the recurrence interval or return period.

keyTerms.gloss: high streamflow that overtops river banks onto adjacent lowlands
keyTerms.quote: A flood is any relatively high streamflow that overtops the natural or artificial banks of a river.

keyTerms.gloss: measured volume of streamflow moving past a point in a given time
keyTerms.quote: Discharge is another term for streamflow; it is the measured volume of water that moves past a point in the river in a given amount of time.

keyTerms.gloss: flat lowland bordering a river that is subject to flooding when banks overtop
keyTerms.quote: The floodplain is the relatively flat lowland that borders a river, usually dry but subject to flooding.

keyTerms.gloss: graph showing changes in discharge or river stage over time
keyTerms.quote: A hydrograph is a graph that shows changes in discharge or river stage over time.
